title: Cough: understanding the pattern and choosing the next step
intro: Coughing helps clear the airways, but an irritating or persistent cough can disturb sleep, work and daily life. A cough is a symptom rather than a single disease. Many follow viral infections and gradually settle; others need treatment of an underlying cause. How it started, how long it lasts and the accompanying symptoms are more useful than choosing a syrup by the sound alone.

sections.heading: Notice the pattern without diagnosing yourself
paragraphs: Record whether the cough is dry or brings up mucus, occurs daily, wakes you at night or follows exercise, meals, smoke or workplace exposure. Note fever, wheeze, breathlessness and any choking episode. Possible causes include respiratory infections, asthma, nasal inflammation, reflux, smoking-related disease and some medicines, including ACE inhibitors. Less common causes can be serious. A new cough after starting a medicine needs discussion, not stopping prescribed treatment independently. A wet cough is not automatically bacterial, and coughing at night alone does not prove asthma.

sections.heading: Urgent signs change the plan immediately
paragraphs: Get emergency help for severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips, collapse or choking with inability to breathe or speak. Coughing up more than a few streaks of blood, or blood together with chest pain or breathing difficulty, also needs emergency assessment. Even small spots of blood should be checked promptly. Seek urgent advice for rapidly worsening cough, chest pain, significant fever, dehydration or feeling very unwell. A child whose cough began after choking on food or an object needs assessment even if the immediate episode settled. Babies with breathing pauses, poor feeding or unusual drowsiness need urgent attention.

sections.heading: Duration matters, but warning signs override the calendar
paragraphs: A cough after an infection can continue for several weeks while other symptoms improve. Arrange assessment if it lasts more than about three weeks, or earlier if worsening or you have important risk factors. In children, a daily wet cough persisting beyond four weeks particularly needs evaluation. Do not simply label repeated weeks of wet coughing as another cold. Unexplained weight loss, night sweats, repeated chest infections or relevant tuberculosis exposure also need assessment. A clinician may examine the chest, review medicines and decide whether chest imaging, lung-function tests or infection testing is appropriate. Not everyone needs every test.

sections.heading: Comfort measures have limits
paragraphs: Avoid smoke and vaping aerosols and reduce known irritants. Regular drinks may soothe the throat; respect any medical fluid restriction. Honey can offer some relief for adults and children over a year old, but never give it to younger babies. Avoid hot steam bowls and choking hazards such as lozenges in young children. Over-the-counter cough products have limited benefit and may cause drowsiness, interactions or accidental double dosing. Ask a pharmacist about age, pregnancy and other medicines; do not use adult products for a child. Pain or fever medicine may improve those symptoms without stopping the cough.

sections.heading: Treat the cause and agree a review plan
paragraphs: Most uncomplicated viral coughs do not need antibiotics. Inhalers, steroids or reflux medicines are not a standard trial for every cough; they should fit the clinical assessment. A diagnosed bacterial infection or chronic airway condition may need specific treatment. A long-lasting unexplained cough may require specialist assessment and tailored cough-control treatment rather than repeated antibiotics. Tell the clinician about sleep loss, urine leakage or fainting with coughing, which deserve support and may affect safety. Ask when improvement is expected, what to do if the plan fails and which symptoms mean earlier reassessment. Persistent symptoms should be taken seriously without assuming the worst cause.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a useful symptom record
examples.text: Ilir has a dry cough after a change in blood-pressure treatment. He records when it began and brings all medicines to the appointment. The clinician checks other causes and decides whether changing treatment is appropriate; Ilir does not stop it himself.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a wet cough that keeps returning
examples.text: A child seems active between colds but has a wet cough every day for several weeks. Her parent notes that there were no cough-free days and arranges a review. The clinician evaluates the persistent pattern instead of recommending repeated shop-bought suppressants.

questions: What causes fit my pattern, and do I need any tests?
Which comfort measures or medicines are suitable for me?
When should the cough improve, and what means I should return earlier?
